E-commerce Delivery and Customer Experience¶

Author: Mohammed Adeen Shaik

Research question¶

How do delivery reliability, seller concentration and reviews vary within the Olist marketplace?

Data and evidence¶

Publisher-provided Olist historical marketplace tables.

Fresh execution on 11 October 2026 using publisher Olist tables. The reporting model contains 99,441 order-level records. Monthly revenue and on-time delivery rates use the exported monthly scorecard. Review-versus-delivery plots are associations within delivered and reviewed records, not evidence of a causal improvement. Customer and seller identifiers are not published in the reading edition.

Measure Value
order rows 99441
monthly buckets 25

Reading guide¶

Read each explanation before its code cell. Run from top to bottom in the documented working directory. A saved chart is an output snapshot, not proof that this notebook was rerun today. The final section collects findings and visual evidence.

Method¶

Orders are the reporting grain. Items, payments and reviews are aggregated before joining so a many-to-many merge cannot inflate order-level totals.

Interpretation limits¶

Review associations do not establish that delivery timing caused a rating. Revenue is product value, not marketplace profit. Seller comparisons require adequate volumes.

E-commerce Operations — Key Visuals¶

Run the marketplace model first. The notebook reviews delivery reliability, freight burden, seller concentration, and review outcomes.

plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False, "font.size": 11})

Guide to code step 2¶

Load the source table. A DataFrame is a spreadsheet-like table in memory. The path must point to the documented input file; loading a file does not validate its contents.

from pathlib import Path
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd

DATA = Path("../data/processed")
orders = pd.read_csv(DATA / "fact_orders.csv", parse_dates=["order_purchase_timestamp"])
monthly = pd.read_csv(DATA / "monthly_marketplace_kpis.csv")
sellers = pd.read_csv(DATA / "seller_scorecard.csv")

Guide to code step 3¶

Read the chart. The axis labels identify units and the grouping defines what is compared. A visual association does not establish cause. Rate charts need denominators; truncated axes can exaggerate small differences.

monthly["purchase_month"] = pd.to_datetime(monthly["purchase_month"])
figure, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5))
axes[0].plot(monthly["purchase_month"], monthly["product_revenue"], color="#2563EB")
axes[0].set(title="Monthly Product Revenue", ylabel="Revenue")
axes[1].plot(monthly["purchase_month"], monthly["on_time_delivery_rate"], color="#059669")
axes[1].set(title="On-time Delivery Rate", ylabel="Rate", ylim=(0, 1))
for axis in axes:
    axis.grid(alpha=0.25)
figure.tight_layout()

Guide to code step 4¶

Read the chart. The axis labels identify units and the grouping defines what is compared. A visual association does not establish cause. Rate charts need denominators; truncated axes can exaggerate small differences.

review_delivery = orders.dropna(subset=["review_score", "delivery_variance_days"])
figure, axis = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
review_delivery.boxplot(column="delivery_variance_days", by="review_score", ax=axis)
axis.set(title="Delivery Variance by Review Score", xlabel="Review score", ylabel="Days vs estimate")
figure.suptitle("")
figure.tight_layout()

Guide to code step 5¶

Read the chart. The axis labels identify units and the grouping defines what is compared. A visual association does not establish cause. Rate charts need denominators; truncated axes can exaggerate small differences.

top = sellers.head(15).sort_values("product_revenue")
figure, axis = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 7))
axis.barh(top["seller_id"], top["product_revenue"], color="#7C3AED")
axis.set(title="Top Sellers by Product Revenue", xlabel="Revenue")
figure.tight_layout()
